description: Germanic Visigothic kingdom in Iberia (418–711) that converted from Arianism to Catholicism at the Third Council of Toledo (589); the Toledo councils synthesised Roman law, Visigothic customary practice, and Church canon law into a sophisticated legal tradition, while the Arab-Berber invasion of 711 destroyed the kingdom but preserved its legal heritage as the foundation of later Castilian and Portuguese law.

temporal.notes: Ended by Umayyad conquest at Battle of Guadalete

lifecycle_phases.description: The Visigoths settle in Aquitaine as Roman foederati under Wallia (418). Under Euric (466–484) the kingdom becomes effectively independent, extending from the Loire to the Strait of Gibraltar. Euric issues the first Germanic law code (Codex Euricianus). Clovis I's Catholic Franks defeat the Arian Visigoths at Vouillé (507), ending the Gallic kingdom and forcing the Visigoths into Hispania.

The Visigoths reestablish their kingdom in Iberia with Toledo as capital. Leovigild (569–586) conquers the Suevic Kingdom (585), defeats the Cantabrians, and suppresses internal revolts. His son Reccared I converts from Arianism to Catholicism at the Third Council of Toledo (589), bringing the kingdom into alliance with the Roman Church and the Hispano-Roman population.

The late Visigothic kingdom suffers endemic succession disputes and aristocratic revolts against royal authority. King Roderic's disputed succession in 710 produces a civil war; the losing faction invites Umayyad forces across the Strait. Tariq ibn Ziyad defeats Roderic at the Battle of Guadalete (711), and within three years the Umayyads have overrun virtually all of Iberia.

rise_factors.description: Visigothic cavalry forces were among the most effective in post-Roman Europe; Euric's military campaigns extended the kingdom from the Pyrenees to the Atlantic, making the Visigoths the dominant power in the western Roman successor world

Reccared I's conversion to Catholicism (589) ended the religious divide between the Arian Germanic elite and the Catholic Hispano-Roman majority, stabilizing the kingdom and winning Church support that provided administrative capacity

The Lex Visigothorum (654) under Recceswinth replaced the dual Roman-Germanic legal system with a single law code for all subjects regardless of ethnic origin, a remarkable legal integration for early medieval Europe

The Liber Iudiciorum (654) unified Visigothic and Roman law under a single code applying to all subjects regardless of ethnic origin, eliminating the dual legal system between Goths and Romans that had plagued other successor states.

Reccared I's conversion from Arianism to Catholicism (589) reconciled the Visigothic ruling class with the Hispano-Roman majority and the Catholic clergy, enabling cooperation between the kingdom's administrative and ecclesiastical elites.

Iberia's exceptional agricultural productivity, Roman granary of the empire, continued under Visigothic rule. Olive oil, wine, and grain surpluses supported urban populations and funded the Visigothic royal court's elaborate patronage.

decline_factors.description: The Visigothic monarchy was elective rather than hereditary; every succession was contested, with at least 14 Visigothic kings assassinated or deposed. Roderic's disputed elevation in 710 directly led to the invitation of Umayyad forces

The Umayyad Caliphate's expansion into North Africa placed a formidable military force immediately across the Strait of Gibraltar; Tariq ibn Ziyad's initial force of ~7,000 was reinforced by Musa ibn Nusayr with 18,000 more troops

The Umayyad conquest (711–718) succeeded with remarkable speed: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed with 7,000 troops, won a single decisive battle (Guadalete), and within three years controlled most of Iberia. The speed reflected Visigothic factional paralysis during a dynastic struggle.

Visigothic kings were elected by nobles, making every reign vulnerable to conspiracy. Between 531 and 711, more than half of Visigothic kings were murdered or deposed. This instability prevented the institutional consolidation needed to resist external pressure.
